passage:
I'm Shalini, and three months into seeing Arvind, I noticed the glow had changed. It didn't vanish; it got quieter, like a song you know by heart.
I started seeing other things. He is late for everything and calls it "flexible". He goes silent for a whole evening when he's stressed, then acts as if nothing happened. And when my cousin chose a lower-paying job teaching in a village school, he called it "wasting a degree", and something in me went still.
He is also the one who stayed up till two helping me fix my thesis charts. Both are true.
My roommate Kavitha asked, "So, do you still get butterflies?"
I said, "Sometimes." Then I heard myself say what I was really thinking: "I care less about the butterflies now. I'm trying to work out if I actually like who he is."

qa.q: What did Arvind call the cousin's choice to teach in a village school?
qa.a: Arvind called it 'wasting a degree'.

qa.q: What did Shalini feel when Arvind called it 'wasting a degree'?
qa.a: Shalini felt uneasy, as if something inside went still, because the comment clashed with values Shalini cares about.

qa.q: What could Shalini do to understand Arvind better at this stage?
qa.a: Shalini could talk with Arvind about that comment and about how each of them sees work and purpose, instead of only noticing it silently.

qa.q: How might Arvind experience these months?
qa.a: Arvind may feel the relationship is going well and not realise Shalini is quietly weighing his habits and values.

grounding: Shows a young adult seeing a partner's habits, moods and values more clearly as the glow fades, and asking whether Arvind himself, not the feeling, is someone to like.

passage:
Student counselling note. Sarita, 20, second year. Came in at the suggestion of her roommate, Himani.
Sarita said nothing is "wrong" with Nitin, whom she has been seeing for four months. But she is noticing things she didn't at first: he keeps money very tight and gets irritated when she spends on friends; he is warm with her but short with waiters; he wants to settle near his parents, while she has always planned to study abroad.
"At first it just felt amazing to be with him," she said. "Now I'm asking whether I actually like the person, not just the feeling." She seemed relieved, and a little sad, saying it.
We talked about how this shift is normal and useful, and that she can raise differences with Nitin directly. She plans to ask him about the study-abroad plan this weekend. Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: Where does Nitin want to settle?
qa.a: Nitin wants to settle near his parents.

qa.q: How did Sarita seem to feel as she described the shift?
qa.a: Sarita seemed relieved and a little sad: relieved to say it aloud, sad that the early glow is fading.

qa.q: What step did Sarita plan, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Sarita planned to ask Nitin about the study-abroad plan this weekend; talking directly about differences shows who he is, not just how the relationship feels.

qa.q: How might Himani have seen things before suggesting counselling?
qa.a: Himani probably noticed Sarita seemed unsettled about the relationship and wanted her to have someone neutral to think it through with.

grounding: Illustrates a student noticing a partner's habits and differing values as they meet more, shifting from how it feels to who he is.

subtype: Stage 3: Getting to know the real person [Actor]
passage:
Tanuja,

I promised I'd tell you how it's going with Vivek, so here's the honest version.

The first month, everything he did was charming. Now it's been four months and I'm seeing the rest of him. He's always twenty minutes late. He goes silent for a whole day when he's upset instead of saying what's wrong. He tips generously, which I love. He also thinks my plan to do a master's in Pune is "a phase," which I don't love at all.

The fizzy feeling has calmed down. I used to ask myself, do I like how I feel around him? Now I'm asking something else: do I like who he actually is, silences and all?

I don't know the answer yet. But I think it's the right question.

Devika

qa.q: How late is Vivek, according to Devika?
qa.a: Always twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What is Devika feeling now that the fizzy feeling has calmed down?
qa.a: Devika feels thoughtful and uncertain, less dazzled, and a bit uneasy about Vivek's silences and his view of the master's plan.

qa.q: What could Devika do to answer her new question?
qa.a: She could talk openly with Vivek about the master's plan and about how he handles being upset, and see how he responds.

qa.q: How might Vivek feel if he read that his view of her plan was "a phase" to her?
qa.a: He might feel surprised or defensive, maybe not realising how much his comment bothered her.

grounding: Devika's letter shows the glow of a new relationship fading as habits and differing values appear, shifting her question from how it feels to who Vivek is.

subtype: Stage 3: Getting to know the real person [Actor]
passage:
You asked what changed with Yamini? I'm Siddharth, and honestly, nothing dramatic. We just started seeing each other a lot.

At first she seemed perfect. Clever, funny, always up for a late-night walk. Then we went on a weekend trip with friends, and I saw her in a bad mood for the first time. She snapped at the driver, then went quiet for an hour. Later she apologised, but it surprised me.

I started noticing other things too. She wants to live in a big city forever; I want to go back to my hometown someday. She's very close to her family; mine is distant.

None of it is a deal-breaker. But the question in my head has shifted. It used to be, "Do I like how she makes me feel?" Now it's, "Do I like who she is, on the bad days too?" And that's a harder question.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth first see Yamini in a bad mood?
qa.a: On a weekend trip with friends.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when Yamini snapped at the driver?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a little unsettled, seeing a side of her he had not seen before.

qa.q: What would help Siddharth at this stage?
qa.a: Talking honestly with Yamini about the differences, like where they want to live, and seeing how they handle it together.

qa.q: How might Yamini see the weekend trip?
qa.a: She might have been embarrassed about snapping and worried about how Siddharth saw her, which may be why she apologised.

grounding: Siddharth gets to know Yamini's moods and differing values, and his question shifts from how the relationship feels to who she really is.

passage:
February. Saurabh and Ayesha had been going out for six weeks, and everything felt golden. She laughed at his jokes; he liked the way she argued with professors.

April, two months on. They were working on a group project together, and Saurabh saw a new Ayesha: organised to the minute, impatient when he was late with his part. When he forgot a deadline, she didn't talk to him for a day. He found himself annoyed, then sheepish, because he had been late.

June, the week after exams. They sat on the steps of the library and talked about next year. She wanted to take a job straight away; he wanted to travel first. Neither was wrong.

Walking home, Saurabh noticed the golden feeling was quieter. But he also noticed he liked the real Ayesha, the one who was sharp and impatient and honest. The question had changed.

qa.q: What were Saurabh and Ayesha working on together in April?
qa.a: A group project.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel when Ayesha didn't talk to him for a day?
qa.a: He felt annoyed, then sheepish, because he knew he had been late.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Saurabh at this stage?
qa.a: He can decide, with open eyes, whether he likes the real Ayesha, sharp and impatient and honest, rather than just the golden feeling.

qa.q: What might Ayesha experience during the group project?
qa.a: She may feel frustrated and stressed when Saurabh is late, worried about the deadline and about their relationship.

grounding: Over months Saurabh sees Ayesha's habits and differing plans, the glow fades, and his question becomes whether he likes who she really is.

subtype: Stage 3: Getting to know the real person [Actor]
passage: You asked how I knew, Shreya, so your Tanuja Masi will tell you. At twenty I was seeing Vivek from the debate club. The first months were long walks and his clever lines. Then we began meeting every day. I saw that he sulked a whole evening if he lost an argument. I saw him keep a waiter standing while he joked with me, never once saying thank you. And when I told him I wanted to work in a village clinic after college, he laughed and said, "You'll grow out of that." The glow did not vanish in one day; it thinned, like a dupatta washed too often. One night, walking home, I stopped asking whether I liked being with him and started asking whether I liked him. That is a harder question, my dear. It took me three more weeks to answer it honestly.

qa.q: What did Vivek say when Tanuja mentioned working in a village clinic?
qa.a: He laughed and said, "You'll grow out of that."

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel as she kept noticing Vivek's sulking and his manner with the waiter?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and quietly disappointed, as the early glow thinned and she saw habits and values that clashed with her own.

qa.q: What turning point does Tanuja reach on that walk home, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She stops asking whether she likes the feeling and asks whether she likes Vivek himself, which lets her judge the real person rather than the early excitement.

qa.q: What would change if Vivek had taken the clinic plan seriously instead of laughing?
qa.a: Tanuja might have felt respected in what she valued, and her harder question could have had a warmer answer, though his sulking and rudeness would still need weighing.

grounding: Shows the early glow fading as a young woman meets her partner often and sees his habits, moods and values more clearly.
